{"id": "74:31/q37", "question": "What further responses does mention of the nineteen elicit?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:31/q37/p1", "position": "Mockers treat the report as a riddle; truth seekers benefit from its wisdom, while arrogant readers reject it.", "reasons": "Elmalılı contrasts receptive believers with diseased deniers; Islahi says mockers presume to know everything, and Asad reports speculation about why Muhammad chose this number."}]}
{"id": "74:31/q38", "question": "How do the four stated responses reinforce one another?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:31/q38/p1", "position": "The sequence magnifies certainty, growth of faith, and freedom from doubt before contrasting the doubters.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī enumerates four effects of the ambiguous passage; al-Zamakhsharī says stated certainty and denied doubt emphasize believers' composure; al-Zarkashī cites the order of scripturalists and believers as progression and the repeated phrase as magnification and awe."}]}

{"id": "74:43/q03", "question": "Why is the nūn omitted in نك?", "turns_on": "Whether the shortened form is explained by the speakers' state or by ease in frequent usage.", "positions": [{"id": "74:43/q03/p1", "position": "Its omission expresses the speakers' extreme distress and deficient natural disposition.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says they are too distressed to utter even a dispensable letter and that the omission signals their lack of a good natural disposition."}, {"id": "74:43/q03/p2", "position": "The nūn is omitted for ease because this form is frequent.", "reasons": "Al-Būrsawī gives frequency and ease as the explanation for نكن becoming نك."}]}
{"id": "74:43/q04", "question": "What Arabic patterns of final weak-letter retention and deletion bear on the shortened wording?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:43/q04/p1", "position": "Final weak letters can be retained or deleted according to noun or verb status, case, pause, and cadence.", "reasons": "Sībawayh says nouns such as qāḍ, ghāz, and ʿamī commonly lose final yāʾ at pause as before tanwīn; nouns are especially prone because deletion also occurs outside cadence. Some Arabs delete it even in definite forms by analogy with indefinite nouns and because yāʾ plus kasra is heavy. Abū al-Khaṭṭāb and Yūnus report trusted speakers retaining it without tanwīn, where clear pronunciation is better; Sībawayh says retention of yāʾ and wāw is more analogical, though deletion is common, and cites Zuhayr for retention in cadence. In the accusative, yāʾ must remain clear because it survives connected speech. The pausal form marrī compensates for not dropping both hamza and yāʾ. Verbs normally retain final yāʾ at pause because it remains in connected speech; lā adri and mā adri are restricted frequent exceptions, compared with lam yak. Qurʾanic cadence and rhyme may delete final weak letters otherwise kept in speech; Sībawayh cites endings at 89:4, 18:64, 40:32, and 13:9."}]}
{"id": "74:43/q05", "question": "Is final yāʾ retained in the vocative yā qāḍī?", "turns_on": "Whether the non-nunated vocative follows al-qāḍī or the vocative tendency to omit material.", "positions": [{"id": "74:43/q05/p1", "position": "The vocative retains yāʾ: yā qāḍī.", "reasons": "Al-Khalīl prefers this by analogy with al-qāḍī because the vocative is not nunated."}, {"id": "74:43/q05/p2", "position": "The vocative drops yāʾ: yā qāḍ.", "reasons": "Yūnus prefers this, and Sībawayh calls it stronger: deletion occurs outside vocatives, and vocatives readily omit material, as in yā ḥār and yā ṣāḥ."}]}

{"id": "75:11/q03", "question": "What does wazar mean, and what does its denial rule out?", "turns_on": "Whether the word names refuge generally, a particular shelter such as a mountain or fortress, a means of escape, or a reported dialectal sense; several sources present the particular shelters as examples of the broad sense.", "positions": [{"id": "75:11/q03/p1", "position": "A refuge or shelter of any kind is unavailable; the word extends to anything that could protect the fugitive.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, Ibn Qutayba, al-Zajjāj, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, al-Biqāʿī, al-Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, and others gloss the denial as no refuge. -Zajjāj, as reported by al-Rāzī, specify an inaccessible mountain; al-Mubarrad adduces Kaʿb ibn Mālik's poem calling swords and spearpoints the people's sole wazar. Ibn ʿAbbās, reported by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, gives fortress or refuge; al-Māwardī specifies refuge from the Fire. Al-Rāzī says nothing shelters one from God's command; al-Samīn cites poetry in which no shelter saves a youth from death and old age. Al-Bayḍāwī calls refuge a metaphor from a mountain stronghold and relates its derivation to burden. Al-Naḥḥās glosses maʾwā as refuge and connects wazīr either to entrusting affairs to a protector or to carried burdens, including precious metals; al-Jishumī connects wazīr to a helper one turns to and compares a wall strengthened by its foundation. Al-Ṭabrisī connects the word with a minister one seeks for help. Al-Ḥasan, reported by al-Suyūṭī, describes a herdsman surprised by cavalry and told to find mountain shelter; Abū Qilāba adds caves. ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm's verse is cited by al-Suyūṭī for Arab usage denying refuge. {"id": "75:11/q06", "question": "How does the denial of refuge fit the surrounding judgment scene?", "turns_on": "The notes draw complementary links: the flight question and return to God, the implied arrival of resurrection, and the reckoning that follows.", "positions": [{"id": "75:11/q06/p1", "position": "It answers the person's question about flight and points to the Lord as the only destination.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies the questioner as the disbeliever mentioned at 75:3 and says he wishes for a place of escape. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reads 75:10–12 together: the terror of resurrection leaves no escape and the final resting place is with the Lord. {"id": "75:16/q02", "question": "Which broader facts about the articulation and form of speech are cited?", "turns_on": "Which articulatory or morphological environment governs the cited speech forms.", "positions": [{"id": "75:16/q02/p1", "position": "Identical consonants may assimilate, conceal, or remain distinct according to movement, word boundaries, and word structure.", "reasons": "Sībawayh favors assimilation when at least five moving segments would follow, citing poetic meter; clear Hijazi articulation remains good. More movements strengthen the preference, and a preceding long vowel counts as movement, as his rhyme example with yāʾ shows. A preceding matching moving consonant and following quiescent consonant also favor assimilation. Across words, distinct articulation remains possible; a quiescent predecessor bars silencing, though concealment with moving weight is possible. Ibn Nūḥ and ism Mūsā preserve word form, unlike intra-word رد and قل. Qurādd/lahāmm cannot be silenced; poems of an unnamed poet and Ghaylān b. Ḥurayth witness concealment. Meccans reportedly do not fully pronounce both tāʾs in 58:9; thawb Bakr favors clarity. Ṣuwaym permits concealment or silence. Final long wāw/yāʾ remain unassimilated before matching initials; speakers can conceal or articulate but cannot silence without losing length, as rhyme confirms. Imperative ikhshi/ikhshū can assimilate because their glides are not long vowels. Two hamzas are normally distinct, although Ibn Abī Isḥāq's assimilation is called poor but permissible. Iftaʿala tāʾs can be shown or concealed, unlike fixed iḥmarra; some Arabs quiesce the first or move the predecessor. Al-Ḥasan's 37:10 reading and Meccan murdifīn reported by al-Khalīl and Hārūn attest alternatives; muqtalīn is rarer and radif dialectal. Initial alif is retained in ألْحمر as hamzat qaṭʿ-like. Assimilation in iqtatalū is acceptable like jaʿal laka. اردد permits no concealment between two still letters."}, {"id": "75:16/q02/p2", "position": "Hamza at pause permits several realizations determined by its preceding sound and case.", "reasons": "Sībawayh records hinted or applied case vowels. Tamīm and Asad often move the predecessor to clarify faint hamza; some Tamīm avoid a faʿl sequence in al-radiʾ. Other Arabs replace final hamza by wāw, yāʾ, or alif by case, as in al-kalʾ/al-wathʾ. The choice should remain consistent. Once the predecessor moves, ordinary pause rules apply; final hamza is not doubled. Hijazi lightening after fatḥa yields alif without ishām; after ḍamma/kasra yields wāw/yāʾ. After a still consonant, softened hamza is deleted and its vowel transferred."}, {"id": "75:16/q02/p3", "position": "Weak letters change form according to position, vowel, suffix, and pattern.", "reasons": "Sībawayh cites taʿayyaṭat and rajaz ʿawṭaṭ for quadriliteral yāʾ becoming wāw. Final radicals are weakest because endings bear inflection and suffixes. Wāw-final imperfects use yafʿulu, yāʾ-final yafʿilu; faʿula occurs with wāw, not yāʾ. Final wāw after ḍamma and yāʾ after kasra resist heavy endings but accept fatḥa. After fatḥa they become alif; before consonantal suffixes they retain their original identity. Declensional final wāw after ḍamma shifts to yāʾ/kasra; consonant-preceded glides behave like sound radicals. Some plurals prefer yāʾ, while wāw after kasra always becomes yāʾ, with ʿAbd Yaghūth's verse cited. An added alif hamzates a final weak radical. Dialectal ghazi/shaqi retain yāʾ; raḍiyū/sarūw depend on vowel retention and two-sukūn avoidance. Lightened hamzated jīʾ/jūyi turns to jī. Deleted weak radicals remain deleted in singular jussives; dual long-vowel markers remain while jussive nūn drops."}, {"id": "75:16/q02/p4", "position": "Weak-medial noun plurals vary by vowel, number, gender, and analogy.", "reasons": "Sībawayh gives afʿāl for small counts of wāw-medial faʿl to avoid heavy afʿul, and fiʿāl/fiʿlān for larger counts; qaws/aqwus and rajaz athwāb preserve rarer afʿul. Yāʾ-medial faʿl likewise takes afʿāl in small counts, often fuʿūl in larger ones. Hollow qāʿ/tāj/jār favor afʿāl and fiʿlān. Yūnus reports feminine dār/sāq/nār with afʿul, but Sībawayh doubts gender alone explains it; dār/sāq also take fuʿul, dīrān, diyār. Nīb avoids yāʾ plus ḍamma. Fīl nouns use afʿāl/fuʿūl, sometimes -ah. Arwāḥ/riyāḥ preserve wāw class patterns. Feminine weak-medial nouns can take -āt or sound-like larger plurals, while nūbah/jawbah/dawlah/qaryah take broken fuʿul. Ḍayʿah/khaymah have nonregular fuʿul by analogy. Qīmah/rībah/dīmah permit sound and broken patterns; nāqah-type favors fiʿāl with fuʿul also; ʾaynūq/qiyam and the poetic tārāt/tīr are exceptional."}, {"id": "75:16/q02/p5", "position": "First-person suffix and pausal pronunciation depend on host structure and articulatory pressure.", "reasons": "Sībawayh distinguishes verb-object -ni from genitive -ī; frequent particles may drop nūn, especially laʿallī, whereas Zayd al-Khayl's poetic laytī is exceptional. ʿAnnī/qadnī/qaṭnī/minnī/ladunnī preserve the nūn-yāʾ marker; ilā/ladā/ʿalā cannot add nūn because their endings cannot move; qaṭ/ʿan/min are fixed like verbs. Some Arabs move a prefinal consonant to avoid adjacent still letters at pause; a Saʿdī poet's al-naqri witnesses this. Vowel harmony or pattern avoidance explains ʿudl/fisl, al-busr, and al-ʿukm; long vowels in Zayd/ʿawn differ. Qalqala qāf/jīm/ṭāʾ/dāl/bāʾ release audibly, sometimes strongly; zāy/ẓāʾ/dhāl/ḍād release softer breath, and other voiceless sounds breathe. Lām/nūn/mīm/ʿayn/ghayn/hamza lack this release. Connected speech suppresses pausal releases, illustrated by ayqiẓ ʿumayran and aḥriz mālan."}]}
